content: Epilepsy is a neurological condition that affects approximately 1% to 3% of the global population, equating to around 50 million individuals worldwide. However, the actual prevalence may be higher, particularly in developing countries where epilepsy is often underreported. While the majority of individuals with epilepsy achieve adequate seizure control through medication, about 25% to 30% of patients are classified as having drug-resistant epilepsy, meaning they continue to experience seizures despite the use of two or more antiepileptic drugs at appropriate dosages. In recent years, researchers have explored the potential of polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation, particularly omega-3 fatty acids such as eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), as a treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy. However, the results of these studies have been inconsistent. Additionally, there are theoretical concerns regarding omega-3 PUFAs, as they are known to reduce platelet aggregation, which could potentially increase the risk of bleeding. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and tolerability of omega-3 PUFA supplementation in controlling seizures in individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases and clinical trial registries was conducted, covering studies up to November 2015. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that investigated the use of PUFAs in this patient population. The outcomes assessed included seizure freedom, seizure reduction, quality of life, adverse effects (including bleeding and gastrointestinal effects), dropout rates, and changes in plasma lipid profiles. Out of eight potentially relevant studies, three met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed. These included two placebo-controlled, double-blind trials conducted in developed countries with adult participants, and one placebo-controlled, single-blind trial conducted in Egypt with pediatric participants. The studies collectively involved 155 participants (85 adults and 70 children). Of these, 78 participants (43 adults and 35 children) were randomized to receive PUFA supplementation, while 77 participants (42 adults and 35 children) received a placebo. The follow-up period for all studies was up to 12 weeks. One study, which exclusively involved children and had a high risk of bias, reported seizure freedom as an outcome. This study found a significantly higher likelihood of seizure freedom in children receiving PUFA supplementation compared to the control group (risk ratio [RR] 20.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.84 to 140.99). Additionally, the same study reported a significant reduction in seizure frequency (at least 50% reduction) in children receiving PUFAs compared to the control group (RR 33.00, 95% CI 4.77 to 228.15). However, when data from the two studies involving adults were pooled, no significant effect of PUFA supplementation on seizure reduction was observed (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.75, I² = 0%, low-quality evidence). None of the included studies assessed adverse effects related to bleeding, which was one of the primary outcomes of interest. Regarding gastrointestinal effects, there were no significant differences between the PUFA and control groups (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.32 to 1.89, low-quality evidence). PUFA supplementation also did not result in significant differences in mean seizure frequency, quality of life, or other side effects. In conclusion, the evidence from this review is insufficient to support the use of PUFA supplementation for the treatment of drug-resistant epilepsy. The limited number of studies, small sample sizes, and methodological limitations highlight the need for further well-designed trials to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of PUFA supplementation in this patient population.
